newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan recovery seen slow despite March trade spurt.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan recovery seen slow despite March trade spurt.

text.p: Taiwan's March trade data issued on Tuesday showed double-digit import and export growth but experts said the figures were not necessarily a sign of a brisk economic recovery.
They said ripple effects from strong capital and material imports and robust high-tech exports may not be seen before the second half.

"The higher-than-expected March exports strongly reflected earlier export orders that were delayed to March," said Core Pacific Securities economist J.C. Yang. "The actual, strong recovery will not be seen until after June."
New monthly finance ministry figures showed Taiwan had a trade surplus of US$555 million in March, down 37.3 percent from US$885 million in March 1996.
March exports were US$10.67 billion, a rise of 18.4 percent from March 1996, while imports rose 24.5 percent to US$10.11 billion -- their first monthly push past US$10 billion.
The export and import figures were higher than economists' respective average forecasts of US$9.672 billion and US$9.082 billion compiled in an April 3 Reuters Poll.
Economists cautioned that export orders received by Taiwan in recent months were not so strong as to portend a rise in export performance significant enough to reignite the economy.
Foreign orders for Taiwan goods rose just 2.03 percent in January to US$9.872 billion compared to January 1996, and slipped an annual 1.7 percent to US$8.697 billion in February.
"A single month's performance cannot count for much. In the first half, the monthly export figures will be up and down," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"A clearer and stronger recovery is not expected until late in the second quarter or the second half when the star electronics industry shows its strength," Huang said.

A finance ministry official attributed the record-high imports mainly to a hefty US$700 million in military outlays arising from the import of two of six Lafayette-class missile frigates bought from France.

"The military spending was what made the big difference in the rise, because military spending in March 1996 was only US$160 million," said Hsu Kuo-chung, director of the ministry's statistics department.
Hsu said imports would have risen only 18.1 percent without the military spending increase.
The frigate order is costing Taiwan about US$3 billion.

Economists said a 25 percent rise in March capital imports and a 17 percent rise for farm and industrial raw materials were clear signs of rising investment and climbing domestic demand, which would ripple through the economy later in 1997.
"Strong growth in March capital goods and raw materials imports supports a general view that the economy is recovering," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
"But whether exports from now on will strengthen (from economists' bearish expectations) to ignite an overall economic recovery remains to be seen," Lin said.

A hard-won acceleration of Taiwan's recovery in the fourth quarter was expected to push gross domestic product growth to 6.28 percent for 1997, but economists now worry whether growth can even hit six percent in the wake of a hog epidemic that on March 20 forced a halt to Taiwan's prodigious pork exports.
The finance ministry said the farm crisis would reduce monthly exports by US$130 million through 1997.
As the epidemic ripples through Taiwan's food-processing and other farm-related industries, economists predict the crisis could slash 1997 GDP growth by anywhere from 0.39 to a full percentage point.
Government economists now forecast 1997 GDP growth of 5.78 to 5.89 percent, up only slightly from 5.71 percent in 1996.
